name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway and Python SDK for Multi-Provider LLM Access
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python SDK from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and model providers, handling routing, budgets, rate limits and observability. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its Python proxy has a history of production incidents, and a Rust rewrite is in early beta, so version pinning and upgrade discipline matter.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and distributed as the repository BerriAI/litellm, with a Python SDK and a proxy server, described on its site as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, now with a Rust core and Python SDK. It appeared as an open source project and its repository shows a last push in October 2026, with roughly 60,000 stars. It occupies the gateway layer of the AI stack, sitting between applications and model providers. Rather than calling each provider's API directly, you point your code at LiteLLM, which normalizes requests into OpenAI or native format and forwards them to the provider you choose. The site describes one control plane spanning an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway, so the same layer handles model traffic, agent invocation and tool access. Its licence is listed as custom, which is worth checking before commercial use.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs LiteLLM does are routing and calling model APIs, tracking spend, enforcing budgets and rate limits, load balancing across providers, applying guardrails, logging requests, and serving as an MCP gateway for tool access. Its documentation shows reliability testing across providers with batch_completion_models_all_responses, which sends one conversation to every model in parallel and returns only the responses that succeeded, dropping models that raise rather than surfacing errors. It is strongest where a team needs one integration point for many providers, per-key, per-team, per-agent and per-customer budgets, and centralized credentials for upstream systems. The site's own benchmarks claim the Rust gateway has the lowest p99 added latency and smallest memory footprint among the gateways it compared, and that it serves about 15 times the throughput of the Python proxy on about 11 times less memory. Those figures come from LiteLLM's own benchmark, so treat them as vendor measurements rather than independent results.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone who has called an LLM API, since the surface is largely OpenAI-compatible and the tutorials show short code examples. Running the proxy in production is a different matter, because it involves deployment, Redis, databases, Kubernetes, authentication through OIDC or SSO/SAML, and upgrade management. The site's incident reports describe failures that required understanding retry behavior, Redis availability, memory growth and prompt caching semantics, which is systems knowledge rather than machine learning mathematics. No deep mathematical background is needed to use the gateway, though understanding tokenization and caching helps when diagnosing cost regressions. For a beginner, the official site offers tutorials, a proxy quick start, and documentation of the management API, but the material assumes familiarity with HTTP services and container deployment.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site documents integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, among more than 100 providers, and the SDK is written in Python. Around the proxy there is an Admin UI, a management API, a Slack admin agent called LiteAdmin built on a LiteAdmin MCP connector that lets an agent handle tasks through the gateway's management API, and support for the A2A JSON-RPC interface for agent invocation. Documentation covers budgets, guardrails, logging, load balancing, OAuth flows for MCP servers, and identity headers such as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id. The repository has a large star count, which suggests a substantial user base, and the blog publishes incident reports and benchmark posts. The site does not give a clear picture of contributor counts, release cadence beyond the incidents described, or third-party plugin ecosystems, so those remain open.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends of that spectrum, but with different tradeoffs. The Python SDK is quick to adopt for experiments, since you can swap provider strings and get cost tracking without rewriting application code. The Python proxy is aimed at production, with budgets, rate limits, guardrails, audit logs and multi-team management, yet the site's own incident reports show that under real load its memory climbs with concurrency, peaking around 359MB, and that pods were OOM-killed in at least one customer outage. The Rust gateway is presented as the answer, committing to sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary, with per-request overhead falling from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms in their benchmark. That Rust gateway is an early beta, so the production-grade performance story is partly a promise rather than a settled fact.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show an enterprise customer running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx, teams using Claude Code against Amazon Bedrock through LiteLLM, and shared-agent deployments with multiple business units, which indicates real production use in organizations rather than only hobby projects. The site describes features built for production such as SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails, and it publishes incident reports with severity levels, which is the behavior of a vendor serving paying customers. Whether LiteLLM is a current standard or a legacy choice is not settled by the material, and the site does not name specific adopters beyond anonymized customers. For someone choosing it for work, the practical signal is that gateway skills transfer across providers, while the version-specific incident history means operational care is part of the job.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python and used from Python applications, and its documentation shows it calling providers over HTTP with httpx rather than through their vendor SDKs, which is why the site could state that the compromised mistralai package was never imported. It is typically deployed alongside Redis for caching and rate limiting, a database for keys and spend records, and Kubernetes or nginx in front of the proxy. It sits beside orchestration frameworks rather than replacing them, since it routes and governs model calls while the application or agent framework decides what to ask. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is a Python control plane in front of many provider APIs, with a Rust core emerging underneath for the hot path, including auth and rate limiting, as the migration proceeds.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site's own incident reports are the clearest statement of limits. A one-line change in August 2026 turned retry breadcrumbs into a structure that doubled in size with every retry, and combined with an unreachable Redis it produced kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS, and thousands of failed requests, with the fix not backported before v1.100.0 was tagged stable. A separate regression silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend two to three times while requests still returned 200s. The Rust gateway is an early beta, so its benchmark claims are not yet independently verified, and the site does not say when the migration will be complete or how the custom licence applies to commercial use. The classifier benchmark the site publishes is explicitly limited, authored with synthetic prompts and without independent review, so it does not establish general accuracy.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
